summary: We develop a macroscopic quasiparticle heating (QPH) model based on modified Rothwarf–Taylor equations for a niobium CPW resonator, predicting that dissipative nonlinearity manifests as a distinctive oval-shaped distortion of the resonance circle in the complex plane. Experimental measurements on a Nb half-wavelength CPW resonator ($f_r = 4.537$ GHz, $L = 13$ mm) across bath temperatures 20 mK to 1.1 K and readout powers up to 0 dBm confirm this signature, with the model reproducing the observed $Q_r$ degradation and resonance distortion over the QPH-dominated regime.
motivation: Dissipative nonlinearities in superconducting resonators limit device performance, particularly in kinetic inductance detectors where high readout power suppresses two-level system noise but can trigger quasiparticle heating losses; identifying the onset and character of this mechanism is crucial for optimizing operating points.
method: We solved the steady-state Rothwarf–Taylor equations with a power-dependent quasiparticle generation rate $\Gamma_r = \eta P_{qp}/(V\Delta)$ to derive a quartic equation for normalized quasiparticle density $u = n_{qp}/n^*$ at each detuning, computing $S_{21}$ trajectories across frequency and power sweeps. Measurements employed a dilution refrigerator setup with VNA readout; quality factors were extracted from resonance magnitude data for bath temperatures above 500 mK where two-level system effects saturate.
result: At base temperature, the model yields global fit parameters $P_c = 0.0311$ mW and $Q_{other}/Q_c = 1.1$, with $Q_{qp,th}/Q_c$ varying from 8.68 at 0.5 K to 5.51 at 1.1 K; the measured $Q_r$ follows the predicted power law $Q_i \propto P_r^{-1/3}$ in the high-power limit, and the oval distortion becomes pronounced above $-40$ dBm, providing a clear diagnostic signature of the QPH regime.
